rules.text: At both case points the crop alternated between corn and soybeans every year from 2008 to 2023, so this is the rotation already in use.

summer_field_share.unit: percent of June-August days with a crop in the field
summer_field_share.parameter: USDA NASS Handbook 628 usual planting and harvesting dates, Illinois (1997)

why.text: At both case points the crop alternated between corn and soybeans every year from 2008 to 2023, so this is the rotation already in use.

evidence.text: The driest summer of 2001-2023 at the case area was 2012: root-zone wetness 0.51, -1.98 standard deviations from the 2001-2023 mean (NASA POWER, GWETROOT, queried 2026-11-14).

In the 4 dry summers of 2001-2023 (2005, 2006, 2012, 2023), this rotation would have had a crop in the field on about 100% of June to August days (usual Illinois planting and harvest dates, USDA NASS Handbook 628, 1997). This measures how much of the summer a crop is exposed, not yield.

gaps.text: No yield data exists for this rotation: county yields cover corn and soybeans as a whole, so the comparison measures stress and exposure, not outcomes.
NASA POWER is a grid of about 50 km: it represents the area, not the plot.

risks.text: In the cited Illinois model, rotations with two crops carried a higher risk of low corn yields in dry weather than rotations with three.
risks.citation: Manski, Socolar et al., "Diversified crop rotations mitigate agricultural losses from dry weather" (manuscript read at https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10554940, Nov 14 2026)

rules.citation: Manski, Socolar et al., "Diversified crop rotations mitigate agricultural losses from dry weather" (manuscript read at https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10554940, Nov 14 2026)
rules.text: In a model of over 2.2 million field-years in Illinois and Minnesota, moving from a 2-crop to a 3-crop rotation lowered the modeled risk of low corn yields in dry weather. In nearly all Illinois counties, over 90% of fields showed reduced risk.

rules.citation: Manski, Socolar et al., "Diversified crop rotations mitigate agricultural losses from dry weather" (manuscript read at https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10554940, Nov 14 2026)
rules.text: In neighboring Logan County, Illinois, the median reduction was about 5 percentage points in the probability of low corn yields in dry conditions.
The study measures how many crops a rotation has, not a specific third crop. Choosing a small grain such as wheat is our assumption and needs local review.

evidence.text: The driest summer of 2001-2023 at the case area was 2012: root-zone wetness 0.51, -1.98 standard deviations from the 2001-2023 mean (NASA POWER, GWETROOT, queried 2026-11-14).

rules.text: In a long-term Nebraska trial, fertilized corn yielded 29% more in two-year rotations and up to 48% more in four-year rotations than continuous corn. These comparisons are against continuous cropping, not against corn-soybean.

rules.text: Across 11 long-term experiments, diverse rotations reduced corn yield losses by 14 to 90% in drought years in half of them, as reported by this study citing earlier work.
The Nebraska trial is a single site under no-till, and the clover was a winter cover crop in only one of four years. Grain sorghum is not grown in the observed McLean fields.

limits: NASA POWER uses a grid of about 50 km: it represents the area, not the plot.
Climate figures are for point A only and summarize June to August.
Yields are county averages for corn and soybeans from USDA surveys. They say nothing about each field or each rotation, so comparisons measure stress and exposure, not outcomes.
Alternative rotations are hypothetical: they do not exist in the observed fields and rest on the cited studies.
